title: Let's Pivot!

Imagine that you know a way to translate reliably from language A to language B, and also a way to translate from B to language C. Then you also know how to translate from A to C: just translate from A to B first, and next from B to C. When a machine translation system uses this strategy, B is called a pivot language.1

NACLO Labs is about to release its groundbreaking new app, NacloTranslate. NacloTranslate can translate between more language pairs than any of its competitors, and it does so by using pivot languages.

Unfortunately, NacloTranslate doesn't always translate totally reliably. In a study, NACLO Labs scientists tried translating ebi from Ejagham to Seri, using Karajá as a pivot language. They hoped to see the app give only the answers kʔe'el and kwassool, which are the results that could be produced from direct (no pivot) translation. But it was observed producing each of these three results on different test runs:

Ejagham (input)Seri (output)
ebikʔe'el
ebikwassool
ebiko'il

D2. NACLO Labs is considering its options for having NacloTranslate translate paban from Tsafiki to English.

a. What are the results of a direct translation? Select all possible answers.
b. What are the results if Karajá is used as a pivot? Select all possible answers.
c. NACLO Labs selects a different pivot language, and the results for paban are green, blue, and black (and no others). Which languages could NACLO Labs be using as pivot? Give all three possible answers.

1 This strategy can be useful when training data is hard to find. Modern machine translators may need to be trained on huge amounts of parallel text — that is, text in one language given alongside its translation in another (much like in some NACLO problems!). Sometimes, A-C parallel text will be hard to find, but A-B and B-C parallel text will be much more common.

hints.text: Everything you need is in the colour-range table from problem (C). A word in one language can be a direct translation of a word in another language exactly when the two words' colour ranges share at least one colour. Start by writing down, for each word in the test runs, the list of colours it can name.

Think about what a pivot does to the set of outputs. Translating A to B gives every B word that overlaps the A word; then translating each of those B words into C gives every C word that overlaps any of them. Because each B word may stretch beyond the original A word's range, the pivot output is always the direct output PLUS possibly extra words — never fewer. So an output that is impossible directly is proof that a pivot was used, and the pivot must be a language containing a single word that overlaps both the source word and that surprising output.

Try the worked example at the top. Ejagham ebi translates directly into Seri kʔe'el and kwassool, because those are the Seri words whose colour ranges overlap ebi. When Karajá is the pivot, ebi first becomes every Karajá word that overlaps it; at least one of those Karajá words reaches into a colour that ebi itself does not cover, and that colour is also covered by Seri ko'il — so ko'il shows up as an extra output. Find that Karajá word in the table; the same 'reaching beyond' logic is what you apply in D1–D3.

explanationHtml:
What the app is actually doing

All of the words in this problem are colour words, and the table from problem (C) tells you which colours each word can name. Languages carve up the colour space differently: English has separate words green, blue and black, while some languages have a single word that covers all the 'cool/dark' colours at once.

Rule for direct translation: a word w of language A can be translated as word v of language C whenever the colour ranges of w and v overlap (they share at least one colour). A single word may therefore have several possible translations, which is why NacloTranslate gives different answers on different runs.

What a pivot changes

With pivot language B, the app does two steps:

  1. Step 1: w (in A) gives every B word whose range overlaps w.
  2. Step 2: each of those B words give every C word whose range overlaps that B word.

Each B word chosen in step 1 touches w, but it may also stick out into colours that w never covered. In step 2, those extra colours can pull in extra C words. So:

The pivot output always contains everything the direct output contains, and sometimes more. A pivot can only add wrong answers; it can never lose a correct one.

That is exactly what happens in the example at the top: Ejagham ebi overlaps Seri kʔe'el and kwassool, so those two are the direct answers. But going through Karajá, one Karajá word that overlaps ebi stretches into a colour that ebi does not cover, and Seri ko'il covers that colour too — so ko'il appears as a third, spurious result.

D1 — spotting the pivot

Look up the colour ranges of the two words in each run.

  • In runs A and C, the two words' ranges overlap, so the output could have come from a plain direct translation — no pivot needed.
  • In run B, Yakan ittem and Guambiano chilga have no colour in common. A direct translator could never pair them, so run B must have used a pivot.

Now, which pivot? You need a language that contains one word x such that x overlaps ittem and x overlaps chilga — a word broad enough to bridge the gap. Scanning the table, three languages have such a word: Bassa, Bété and Ejagham (all of them have very few, very wide colour terms). Any one of these is an acceptable answer.

D2 — counting the outputs

a. Direct translation of Tsafiki paban into English: list the English words whose range overlaps paban. Those are blue and black.

b. With Karajá as pivot: first find every Karajá word overlapping paban. Those Karajá words reach further than paban does, into green and yellow territory. Translating them into English therefore returns yellow, green, blue, black — the two correct answers plus two extras. Notice how this illustrates the rule: the pivot set contains the direct set.

c. Now we want the output to be exactly green, blue, black: one extra word (green) compared with the direct answer, and no yellow. So the pivot language must have word(s) overlapping paban that extend into green but stop short of yellow (and don't reach white, red, etc.). Checking each candidate language in the table gives three that work: Seri, Matsés and Ejagham.

D3 — matching six pivots

For each run, the recipe is the same: a pivot language works only if it has a single word that overlaps both the source word and the printed output word (that is how the output could survive the two-step journey). Compute the colour range of both words, then test the six options A–F. Because each option is used exactly once, you can also use elimination: nail down the runs with only one possible bridging language first, then remove those options from the remaining runs.

For example, in a run where the two words are separated by a large gap in the colour space, only a language with very broad terms (Bassa or Bété) can bridge it; a language with many narrow terms like English can only bridge small gaps.

Carrying this out for all six runs gives:

Run123456
PivotC. BétéD. EnglishF. TsafikiE. TeribeB. BassaA. Apinaye

The big idea

Real machine-translation systems use pivot languages when they lack parallel text (the same text in two languages) for a pair of languages. This problem shows the hidden cost: every time you pass through a language whose words are 'wider' than the original, meaning leaks in. Errors accumulate, and the set of possible outputs grows — a pivot never sharpens a translation, it can only blur it.
